prompt: Which ionization methods do mass spectrometry analyses of sensitive biological samples typically use?

choices.text: ESI (electrospray) or MALDI (matrix-assisted laser desorption)
Electron-impact ionization with a beam of about 70 eV
choices.why: Biological samples rarely use electron-impact, magnetic-sector methods; they cause heavy fragmentation.

choices.text: Electron impact followed by a double-focusing magnetic analyzer
choices.why: Magnetic-sector instruments are rarely used for sensitive biological samples. ESI or MALDI with a TOF analyzer is typical.

choices.text: Neutralizing the sample so the magnetic field can't deflect it
choices.why: Neutral molecules can't be sorted or detected. ESI and MALDI give charged, protonated molecules.

explanation: MS analyses of sensitive biological samples rarely use magnetic-sector instruments. Instead they typically use electrospray ionization (ESI) or matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization (MALDI), usually linked to a time-of-flight (TOF) mass analyzer.

prompt: What do ESI and MALDI have in common?

choices.text: Both give charged molecules with little fragmentation
Both bombard the sample with high-energy electrons
choices.why: That is electron-impact ionization, which causes heavy fragmentation.

choices.text: Both remove an electron from the sample to give cation radicals
choices.why: Both add protons to the sample, giving variably protonated molecules, M + H_n^{n+}.

choices.text: Both sort the ions they form with a strong magnetic field
choices.why: ESI and MALDI are ionization methods. They are typically linked to a time-of-flight analyzer, not a magnetic sector.

explanation: Both ESI and MALDI are soft ionization methods that produce charged molecules with little fragmentation, even for sensitive biological samples of very high molecular weight.

prompt: In an electrospray ionization (ESI) source, how do the sample molecules become charged?

choices.text: They gain protons from charged solvent molecules in the droplets
A laser ionizes a matrix compound, which then protonates them
choices.why: That describes MALDI, where the sample is adsorbed onto a matrix such as 2,5-dihydroxybenzoic acid.

choices.text: A beam of high-energy electrons knocks out one of their electrons
choices.why: That is electron-impact ionization, which ESI avoids.

choices.text: They lose protons to the solvent and become negative ions
choices.why: They gain one or more protons and become positive ions.

explanation: In an ESI source, the sample solution is subjected to a high voltage as it exits a tube, which charges the droplets. The sample molecules gain one or more protons from charged solvent molecules, and the volatile solvent evaporates, leaving variably protonated sample molecules (M + H_n^{n+}).

prompt: In a MALDI source, what is the role of a compound such as 2,5-dihydroxybenzoic acid?

choices.text: A laser ionizes it, and it then protonates the sample
It is the solvent that evaporates from charged droplets
choices.why: Charged, evaporating droplets describe ESI. In MALDI the sample is adsorbed onto a matrix compound.

choices.text: It is the detector surface that counts the separated ions
choices.why: It is part of the ionization source, not the detector.

choices.text: It is a reference compound fragmented to calibrate masses
choices.why: The section describes it as the matrix the sample is adsorbed onto, which transfers energy and a proton to the sample.

explanation: In a MALDI source, the sample is adsorbed onto a suitable matrix compound, such as 2,5-dihydroxybenzoic acid, which is ionized by a short burst of laser light. The matrix then transfers the energy to the sample and protonates it, forming M + H_n^{n+} ions.

prompt: In a time-of-flight analyzer, every ion in a packet gets the same kick of energy. How are ions of different mass separated?

choices.text: Lighter ions move faster and reach the end sooner
Heavier ions move faster because they carry more energy
choices.why: Every ion gets the same energy, E = mv^2/2, so the heavier ones move more slowly.

choices.text: A magnetic field in the drift tube bends lighter ions more
choices.why: The drift tube is simply an electrically grounded metal tube. Ions separate by how long their flight takes.

choices.text: An oscillating field lets only one m/z through at a time
choices.why: That describes a quadrupole mass analyzer.

explanation: Each ion gets the same energy, E = mv^2/2, so it moves with velocity v = √(2E/m). Lighter molecules move faster and heavier ones slower, so in the drift tube they separate and take different amounts of time to complete their flight.

prompt: In a TOF analyzer every singly charged ion gets the same energy, so its velocity is v = √(2E/m). How many times faster does an ion of mass 1,000 amu move than an ion of mass 9,000 amu?
explanation: v is proportional to 1/√m, so the speed ratio is √(9,000/1,000) = √9 = 3. The lighter ion moves 3 times as fast and finishes its flight first.

prompt: With a time-of-flight instrument, protein samples up to how many atomic mass units can be separated?
explanation: The TOF technique is considerably more sensitive than the magnetic-sector alternative: protein samples of up to 100 kilodaltons (100,000 amu) can be separated.

prompt: Protein samples up to 100,000 amu can be separated by a TOF instrument with a mass accuracy of how many parts per million (ppm)?
explanation: Protein samples of up to 100 kilodaltons (100,000 amu) can be separated with a mass accuracy of 3 ppm.

prompt: Biochemists usually report masses in daltons (Da). How does a dalton compare with an atomic mass unit?

choices.text: They are equivalent: 1 Da = 1 amu
1 Da = 1000 amu
choices.why: 1000 amu is a kilodalton. The dalton and the amu are the same size.

choices.text: 1 Da is the mass of one protein molecule
choices.why: A dalton is a unit of mass equal to 1 amu; a protein such as lysozyme has a mass of thousands of daltons.

choices.text: 1 Da = 100 amu
choices.why: The two units are the same size: 1 dalton = 1 amu.

explanation: Biochemists generally use the unit dalton, abbreviated Da, instead of amu, although the two are equivalent (1 dalton = 1 amu).

prompt: The MALDI–TOF spectrum of chicken egg-white lysozyme shows peaks at 14,306.7578 and 28,614.2188 daltons. What do these peaks represent?

choices.text: The protonated protein, M + H^+, and a dimer of the protein
The molecular ion, M^+, and its M + 2 isotope peak
choices.why: An M + 2 peak would be only 2 units higher. 28,614 is about twice 14,306.

choices.text: The protein with one added proton and with two added protons
choices.why: Adding protons raises the charge, which puts the extra protonated species at lower m/z values, not at about double.

choices.text: Two large fragments formed when the protein breaks apart
choices.why: Fragments would be lighter than the protein. The peak at 28,614 is heavier, about twice the protein's mass.

explanation: In the MALDI–TOF spectrum of lysozyme (MW = 14,306.7578 Da), the peak at 14,306.7578 daltons is the monoprotonated protein, M + H^+, and the peak at 28,614.2188 daltons is an impurity formed by dimerization of the protein. Other peaks at lower m/z values are various protonated species, M + H_n^{n+}.
